Fire Point's ballistic program encompasses two missiles built for distinct roles — tactical and strategic.

FP-7 — tactical ballistic missile. Range — up to 250 km, warhead mass — up to 200 kg.

FP-7 is Fire Point's first ballistic missile. Its mission is to strike Russian military bases and rear-area targets near the front line, where Russian units draw equipment, ammunition, and reinforcements. FP-9 — ballistic missile for strategic-scale missions. Range — up to 850 km, warhead mass — up to 800 kg.

RT @oegerikus: We’ve raised over $270 million for @Xbow.
3 pieces of advice I’d give to every founder:

1. The partner matters more than the fund.

You are not working with the entire VC fund. You are working with one person for many years, so choose the right one.

I'’ve been lucky to have @Konstantine  from day zero, and then @apoorv03, @rsayar and @SanjotMalhi. Each brings a unique perspective that helps me run the company better.

2. Know what the money buys before you raise.

Before you raise, know exactly where you will spend it. For us it buys speed. XBOW is growing at a furious pace in a competitive market, and the funding lets us hire the best people and build the product faster. It also helps us stay ahead of attackers who already leverage AI to find exploits.

3. Only raise when you have a clear plan for the money.

Raising a round is not a requirement for success. My first company, Semmle, grew organically over 13 years before GitHub acquired it. The pace was slow and deliberate, and we got away with raising very little.

I’m sure others have different advice, I’d be curious to hear it.

items.content:
Agentic Offensive Frameworks have cost me a few nights of sleep over the last three months.

I'm convinced we're entering a new era in cybersecurity, and to be honest, it frightens me. I expect a lot of friction and some havoc, and I'm not sure how many organizations can withstand it.

The way I see it, the internet as we know it only worked because nobody had the time to look closely at most of it. Every system got scanned, but almost nothing got a careful second look. #AOFs remove that limit. Now everything gets that look. And I don't just mean source code, vulnerabilities and exploits. The whole threat landscape shifts.

So I kept asking myself what this means for the future, and for the things we build tomorrow. I came up with a term for my answer: defensive minimalism. 
I think it's the way forward.

In the post I explain what I see as the core problems, and why I think tomorrow will look very different from today in many ways.

Blog

items.content:
RT @HackingLZ: Monday thoughts

I don’t see offensive agentic frameworks getting quiet anytime soon. If your endgame is deploying ransomware or stealing files and demanding payment, you only need to stay quiet long enough to get there. And stealth comes at a cost. The less an agent can poke around, the less context it has to work with.  You get stealth or coverage not both. 

The more public the framework, the faster its baked in opsec becomes an EDR signature. Ship a modified Impacket and defenders get a copy too. That’s a big reason a lot of red teams stopped publishing tools.

Internally, these public frameworks already struggle with EDR and identity controls. Blocking suspicious activity and killing processes by default would go a long way. Stronger default policies is the win here. 

Externally, it’s a different story. Plenty of web apps and APIs have never been fully tested, and LLMs still crank out insecure code. We’ve seen plenty of AI pilled startups get popped this year.

I think this gets worse before it gets better. Eventually, more companies will go back to treating the internet as hostile and blocking the attacks they’ve gotten used to ignoring. That part probably won’t go over well with the bug bounty crowd.

RT @spycraft101: In January 2024 the Dutch newspaper De Volkskrant revealed the agent who delivered the infamous Stuxnet virus into the Iranian Natanz nuclear research facility was not an Iranian technician as originally believed, but a Dutch engineer named Erik van Sabben.

Van Sabben worked for TTS International, a Dubai-based company which supplied parts for the Iranian oil and gas industry. He was recruited by the Dutch AIVD intelligence service in 2005, and his family recalls that he was skilled with computers and an adventurous risk-taker. He was also married to an Iranian woman.

Although details are still unclear, the AIVD made Van Sabben available for a joint operation with the American NSA and Israeli Mossad, with the goal of sabotaging the Iranian nuclear weapons program. However, the AIVD was not aware that Van Sabben would be delivering a digital weapon which would essentially usher in an entirely new form of warfare. When the ramifications of Stuxnet became clear, both the AIVD and the Dutch government felt blindsided.

In late 2008 Van Sabben traveled with his wife to Tehran for a planned ten-day trip. However, after just a single day in country he suddenly changed his mind and wanted to leave immediately. It now appears that Van Sabben was able to access the underground nuclear research facility at Natanz at some point and install Stuxnet via a digital water pump.

Stuxnet was a next-generation cyber weapon which targeted the programmable logic control computers regulating the Natanz centrifuges, causing them to spin out of control and self-destruct at seemingly random times with no apparent cause. One cybersecurity expert described it as the equivalent of an “F-35 jet appearing over a World War I battlefield.”

By 2010, Stuxnet had destroyed more than 1,000 centrifuges at the facility. Stuxnet has continued to surface in the years since its discovery and has propagated into multiple versions of itself.

Two weeks after he left Iran, Erik Van Sabben was killed in a single-vehicle motorcycle accident in Dubai, in which he suffered a broken neck.
